tasks.prompt: Hopkins: be specific
tasks.body: Claude Hopkins (Scientific Advertising, 1923) argued that general claims like 'best in the world' slide off the reader, while a definite fact is believed. A specific number signals that you measured something. Paraphrase: platitudes are taken with a discount; specifics are accepted as truth.
tasks.example: Hopkins' own Schlitz campaign is the classic: instead of claiming 'pure beer', he described the process (filtered air, artesian wells, steam-cleaned bottles) that every brewery used but none had told the public.

'Laser hair removal with a 4-step consultation and patch test before your first session'

tasks.prompt: Hopkins: the headline picks the reader
tasks.body: Hopkins compared headlines to a salesperson calling out to a crowd: you shout to the people you want, so the right ones turn their heads. A headline that names the reader (or their situation) filters for buyers instead of trying to please everyone.
tasks.example: In the Upworthy archive, 'If You Drink Coffee, Here's A Fact You Really Need To Wake-Up To' beat 'How Your Morning Latte Is Making The Earth Thirsty' on CTR with the same image (see Track 2).

drill.q: For a dental clinic ad, which opening line picks the reader better?
options: 'Do you own a smile?'
'Clinic owners in Stockholm: is your Google listing sending patients to the clinic next door?'
drill.why: It names the exact reader (clinic owners in Stockholm) and their situation. 'Do you own a smile?' calls everyone and no one.

tasks.explanation: It names the exact reader (clinic owners in Stockholm) and their situation. 'Do you own a smile?' calls everyone and no one.

tasks.title: Hopkins: the headline picks the reader

tasks.prompt: Hopkins: samples, service and testing
tasks.body: Hopkins pushed samples and free trials because they let the product sell itself, and he treated every ad as a test measured by coupons returned. 'Offer service' — give the reader something useful — rather than begging for a purchase.
tasks.example: Caples' piano ad and Sherwin Cody's English ad both asked only for a free booklet or lesson first — a free first step, measured by returned coupons.

'Book a 60-minute strategy call to hear about our services'
drill.why: The report gives value up front and demonstrates expertise (a sample). The call asks for time before any value.

tasks.prompt: Ogilvy: the headline is 80 cents of your dollar
tasks.body: Ogilvy, Confessions of an Advertising Man: "On the average, five times as many people read the headline as read the body copy. When you have written your headline, you have spent eighty cents out of your dollar." On Meta, the 'headline' is effectively the first line of primary text plus the first frame of the creative.
tasks.example: Bing's 2012 test: moving ad text into the title (a bigger headline) raised revenue 12% (HBR).

tasks.prompt: Ogilvy: one big, specific fact

tasks.example: The ad is widely credited with a large sales increase in 1958 (sources differ on the size — treat as reported, not tested).

tasks.prompt: Caples: self-interest, news, curiosity
tasks.body: John Caples (Tested Advertising Methods) grouped winning headlines into self-interest (what's in it for me), news (something new), and curiosity — warning that curiosity alone is weak; it must be combined with self-interest.
tasks.example: Caples' own 1926 'They Laughed When I Sat Down at the Piano...' combined a dramatic story (curiosity) with the reader's wish to be admired (self-interest), and brought record coupon returns (Advertising Hall of Fame).

drill.why: It teases (which 3?) and is clearly useful to the reader. Pure curiosity ('you won't believe this') gives no reason to care.

tasks.explanation: It teases (which 3?) and is clearly useful to the reader. Pure curiosity ('you won't believe this') gives no reason to care.

tasks.prompt: Schwartz: awareness levels
tasks.body: Eugene Schwartz (Breakthrough Advertising) described five levels: unaware, problem-aware, solution-aware, product-aware, most-aware. Your headline should start where the reader's mind already is. Cold clinic owners seeing a Meta ad are usually problem-aware at best ('fewer bookings') — not aware that their Google Business Profile is the cause.
tasks.example: Summary of the model: Personal MBA, 'Levels of Awareness'.

drill.q: A clinic owner who has never thought about Google Maps is…
options: Product-aware: show the 4,900 kr price first
Unaware/problem-aware: start with the symptom (empty slots, patients choosing competitors) and the free check
drill.why: Price-first works for the most-aware. Unaware readers need the problem made visible first.

tasks.explanation: Price-first works for the most-aware. Unaware readers need the problem made visible first.
tasks.source_name: Personal MBA: Levels of Awareness (summary of Schwartz, Breakthrough Advertising)
tasks.title: Schwartz: awareness levels

tasks.prompt: Schwartz: market sophistication
tasks.body: When a market has heard every claim ('more leads!'), a bigger claim stops working. Schwartz's stages: make the claim → enlarge it → introduce a mechanism (HOW it works) → enlarge the mechanism → identification (speak to who they are). Agency marketing to clinics is a very sophisticated market.

drill.q: Clinic owners get 'we'll double your leads' messages weekly. Which is a stage-3 (mechanism) message?
options: 'We'll TRIPLE your leads!'
'Most clinics lose Maps clicks because of 3 missing profile fields. We fix them in one go.'
drill.why: It explains the mechanism (missing fields → lost clicks) instead of shouting a bigger number.

tasks.explanation: It explains the mechanism (missing fields → lost clicks) instead of shouting a bigger number.
tasks.source_name: NordicCopy: What is Market Sophistication? (summary of Schwartz)
tasks.title: Schwartz: market sophistication

tasks.prompt: Hormozi: the value equation
tasks.body: Alex Hormozi ($100M Offers): Value = (Dream outcome × Perceived likelihood of achievement) ÷ (Time delay × Effort & sacrifice). Beginners only inflate the top (bigger promises). Stronger offers shrink the bottom: faster, less work for the buyer.
tasks.example: Highrise's winning test literally reduced 'time delay' and 'effort' in the headline/subhead: '30-day Free Trial' + 'Sign-up takes less than 60 seconds' (+30%).

drill.q: Which change improves the bottom of the equation for the 4,900 kr Google profile fix?
options: 'Double your patients!'

drill.why: It reduces effort & sacrifice for the owner. The first just inflates the promise.

tasks.explanation: It reduces effort & sacrifice for the owner. The first just inflates the promise.
tasks.source_name: Acquisition.com free training ($100M Offers, value equation)
tasks.title: Hormozi: the value equation

tasks.prompt: Meta health policy for clinic ads
tasks.body: Meta's Health & Wellness standard prohibits 'statements of inferiority about physical appearance' and restricts cosmetic procedure / weight ads to 18+. Also avoid implying you know the viewer's personal attributes ('Are YOU overweight?'). Safe pattern: describe the service and the process; avoid shaming and unqualified timed result promises.

tasks.prompt: Cold email basics
tasks.body: Published data agree on a few patterns: short subject lines (2–4 words, Belkins), relevant personalization (Belkins: 7% vs 3% reply), simple language (Boomerang), and a low-friction interest CTA for strangers (Gong). Plain text, one ask, written for one person.
tasks.example: Gong Labs CTA study (304,174 emails) and Belkins subject-line study (5.5M emails).
